name: Dana Alvarez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for having me, Dana. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Luis and I run Brackenridge Farm, and I'm the one who runs the business side and the stock. We've got 150 grass-fed beef cattle, 500 ewes and some barley, and we sell most of the meat ourselves, through our own butchery, a farm shop and online meat boxes. My day starts at six with a coffee and the overnight orders, which my AI assistant has already sorted into a cutting list for our butcher. Then I check the cattle on my phone, because they wear GPS collars that move them between paddocks with sound cues instead of fences, and then I'm out on the hill.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you love, and what wears you down?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love that we built this ourselves, from a farm that sold store lambs at the market for whatever the auctioneer said. I love a Saturday when the shop's full and people tell me the lamb was the best they've had. What wears me down is the hours, and the bank loan we took for the butchery. And regulation, honestly, every year there's a new form from people who've never sold a chop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. I'll read it as it's written. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the tools are still worth using, even if they're not a revolution. I'd post on the farm's page about how AI helps a family business compete with the supermarkets. At church I'd say hard work still beats hype.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm fine. The shop and meat boxes are growing about ten percent a year, the loan's on track, and Luis and I aren't afraid of work. The only real worry is a bad year, a dry summer or a customer scare, but we've got a few months' savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using AI for orders, cutting lists, social posts and grazing plans, because it saves me a full day a week. I'd put money into a second cold room next spring, so we can take on two more restaurants. Otherwise I'd keep doing what we're doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Busy, but calm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a customer scare. What does that mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A food scare on the news, or one bad review that spreads, can halve our online orders for a month. It happened once with a supermarket recall that had nothing to do with us. We got through it, but it taught me to keep a cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who works for you, and how do you think about them?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We've got two farmhands, a butcher called Owen and three part-timers in the shop. Owen is training a young apprentice, Liam, which I'm proud of. I'd rather give a local lad a trade than a handout.

I'd post that AI helps a **family business** compete with supermarkets.
think: The **shop and meat boxes** grow about ten percent a year, so I'm fine.
The only real worry is a **bad year**, like a dry summer or a food scare.
do: Keep using **AI** for orders, cutting lists, posts and grazing plans.
Put money into a **second cold room** next spring.

fieldNote: A confident **owner-operator** with a growing direct-sales business.

steps.text: Keep using AI for orders, cutting lists and grazing plans
Build a second cold room next spring for two more restaurants
Carry on running the farm shop and meat boxes as now

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good news for anyone willing to work and learn. Family businesses can move faster than big companies. I'd say the market will reward people who adapt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think it's great for us. Customer emails, booking deliveries, stock ordering, all of that goes to AI, and I can spend more time with customers and the cattle. The worry is my customers: if lots of office workers in town lose jobs, they buy less of our good meat.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd set up an AI system to answer customer messages and plan delivery routes this winter. I'd look at a robot that can weigh and sort lambs, there's a firm trialling one. And I'd start a farm butchery course for the public, three Saturdays a year, because people want real skills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Excited, but watching the town.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do if the town's office jobs did shrink?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd offer smaller boxes at lower prices so people could still buy local. I'd lean more on restaurants and the tourist trade. The business has to follow the customers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would anyone at Brackenridge lose out?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe Sue in the shop, who does the phone orders. I'd move her to the counter and the courses, because she's the face customers know. I'd never let a computer replace the person my customers trust.

say: I'd say it's **good news** for anyone willing to work and learn.
I'd say **the market rewards** people who adapt.
think: AI takes the **emails and ordering**, freeing time for customers and cattle.
The worry is **town office workers** losing jobs and buying less meat.
do: Set up **AI customer messaging** and delivery routes this winter.
Look at a **robot lamb-weigher** a local firm is trialling.
Start public **butchery courses** three Saturdays a year.

fieldNote: Sees Steady Disruption as **good for her** and her business.
Notices the knock-on risk: her **customers' jobs**.
Plans **cheaper boxes** to follow customers if incomes fall.
Keeps **Sue** as the trusted face of the shop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say businesses need to move fast, and that families should look after each other. I'd say government should keep out of the way, mostly, but stop the giant firms from owning everything. I'd say it on the farm page and at church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, 2028 is fine for my desk work, AI does it already. 2031 is the problem: robot farms producing cheap meat, and half the town out of work since 2028 with less to spend. Our whole model depends on people paying more for local, and I'm not sure they could.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd pay down the butchery loan as fast as possible, starting now. I'd get our own robots early, a robot shepherd or feeder, so our costs drop before the price war. And I'd grow the farm stays and courses, because people still pay for experiences.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I'd still be working, but at night it would bother me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said government should keep out of the way but stop giant firms. Isn't that a contradiction?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I believe in free markets, but a market where three companies own every robot isn't free. I'd want fair rules, not handouts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mateo and Rosa?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Mateo, who's fourteen, to learn how to run a business and fix a machine. Rosa's nine, she'd just want the lambs to be safe. I'd tell them the farm isn't going anywhere, even if it changes.

I'd say government should stay out, but stop **giant firms** owning everything.
think: **2031** brings robot farms with cheap meat and a town out of work.
Our model depends on people **paying more for local**, and they may not.

fieldNote: Her own desk work is fine; the threat is **cheap robot meat** and lost customers.
Names a tension between **free markets** and monopoly, and owns it.
Moves fast: **pay debt**, buy robots, grow experiences.
Reassures her kids that **the farm stays**.

steps.text: Pay down the butchery loan as fast as possible

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent warning for a business that pays attention. I'd tell other farm shops to start planning now. I'd say adapt or get left behind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel a bit better. 2031 for AGI and 2034 for robots means I can pay off the butchery loan and get the farm stays established. I'd be 51 and Mateo would be 21.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First year, I'd write a five-year plan with AI and Luis, kitchen table and laptop. I'd buy a small robot for the sheep when one is ready, around 2030. And I'd invest in two farm-stay cabins, because people will want time on a real farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but it's an uneasy I can work with.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Luis go along with it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis is slower than me with new things, but he trusts the numbers. If I show him the cabins pay back in five years, he'll build them himself. He's a good builder.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would your customers want in 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My customers in 2034 will want honest food from people they can see. I don't know if enough of them will be able to afford it. That's the bit I can't plan for.

say: I'd say **five years** is a decent warning for a business that pays attention.
I'd tell other farm shops to **adapt** or get left behind.
think: Five years lets me pay off the **butchery loan** before the robots.
I can't plan for whether customers can **still afford** honest food.
do: Write a **five-year plan** with Luis using AI.
feel: **Uneasy**, but in a way she can work with.
S3.quote: My customers in 2034 will want honest food from people they can see. I don't know if enough of them will be able to afford it.
fieldNote: Five years gives her a **workable plan**.
The unknown is **customer spending**, not her own skill.
Luis is the **slower partner**, won over by numbers.

steps.text: Write a five-year farm plan with Luis using AI

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and final picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift for businesses that plan. I'd say families and communities will get through it, as they always have. I'd keep posting about the farm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel calm. I'd be 53 in 2039, the loans paid, the kids grown. Brackenridge could be a robot-helped farm with a thriving shop and stays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going and keep investing a bit each year. I'd encourage Mateo to study agricultural business or engineering. And I'd keep learning every new tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Hopeful, really.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would still worry you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether the town's families are still working. A farm shop needs customers with jobs. That's out of my hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Brackenridge to look like in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd want Brackenridge to be a farm where robots do the heavy work and people do the caring, the selling and the teaching. With Mateo or Rosa running it if they want to. And Owen still cutting meat, because nobody does it better.

say: I'd say **ten years** is a gift for businesses that plan.
I'd say **families and communities** will get through it, as always.
think: At **53** in 2039, with loans paid and kids grown, I'd feel secure.
Brackenridge could be a **robot-helped farm** with a thriving shop.
do: Keep **investing a bit** each year in the farm.
Encourage **Mateo** towards agricultural business or engineering.
S4.quote: A farm shop needs customers with jobs.
fieldNote: Ten years makes her **calm and hopeful**.
Pictures robots doing **heavy work**, people doing the caring.
Her one worry is **customers' jobs**, outside her control.
Plans for **Mateo's studies** to carry the farm on.

steps.text: Keep investing a little each year in Brackenridge

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because my customers lose their jobs before I've paid off the loan. What would help is fair rules so a few big companies can't own all the robots, and help for local businesses to buy their own. Not handouts, just a level field.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who'll buy the food. Everyone talks about who makes it, robots or people. But if nobody has a wage, nobody buys my lamb, however good it is.

headlineQuote: If nobody has a wage, nobody buys my lamb, however good it is.
portrait: **Dana Alvarez**, 43, runs **Brackenridge Farm** with Luis, selling beef and lamb direct.
She uses **AI every day** and GPS collars to move cattle without fences.
She's **calm** in the slower scenarios and sees AI as a chance to compete.
Fast AGI makes her **anxious** because cheap robot meat and jobless customers threaten sales.
She believes in **free markets** but wants rules stopping a few firms owning every robot.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because customers lose jobs before the butchery loan is paid.
whatWouldHelp: **Fair rules** so a few big companies can't own all the robots.
